item.research_question: Can an Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy coating be successfully fabricated on an AZ91D magnesium alloy substrate via laser cladding to improve its wear and corrosion resistance, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
item.material_system: Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy coating on AZ91D magnesium alloy substrate; mixed elemental powders of Cu, Ni, Al, Co, Cr, and Fe (99 wt % purity, 48–75 μm particle size)
item.processing_route: Laser cladding using a TR050 type CO2 high-power laser under 99.999% argon protection; mixed powders ball milled, preset with 4 vol % PVA solution (0.6 mm thickness); laser power 3000 W, scanning speed 10 mm/s, spot diameter 4 mm, overlap rate 25%
item.test_conditions: Dry sliding wear: 98 N load, 0.4187 m/s speed, 75 mins duration (1884 m distance), bearing steel (AISI52100) friction pair; Corrosion: potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt % NaCl solution, −2.5 V to 1.5 V range, 1 mV/s scan rate; Microhardness: 100 g load, 15 s dwell time
key_findings: The coating consists of a simple FCC solid solution phase with fine dendritic microstructure.
Microhardness of the coating is HV0.1365, approximately 3.7 times higher than the AZ91D matrix (HV0.198).
The coating's wear weight loss is about 2.5 times smaller than that of the AZ91D matrix.
Wear rate of the coating is 11.93 μg/s compared to 30.38 μg/s for the AZ91D matrix.
The coating exhibits abrasive wear, whereas the AZ91D matrix exhibits adhesive wear.
Corrosion potential (Ecorr) of the coating is −0.998 V, significantly more positive than the AZ91D matrix (−1.46 V).
Corrosion current density (icorr) of the coating is 1.60 × 10−4 A/cm2, lower than the AZ91D matrix (6.20 × 10−4 A/cm2).
Copper segregates significantly in the inter-dendrite regions due to positive mixing enthalpies with other elements.
item.mechanism: The high microhardness and wear resistance are attributed to solid solution strengthening and fine grain strengthening from the rapid solidification process, combined with the alloy's superior work-hardening capacity which allows the coating to shear off steel debris that then acts as abrasive particles. The improved corrosion resistance is attributed to the formation of dense chromium, aluminum, and nickel oxides on the surface, which protect against the aggressive attack that occurs on the loose, porous magnesium oxide film of the AZ91D substrate.
item.limitations: The authors state that the specific Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi composition selected is not superior to other high-entropy compositions and was chosen only for its known good corrosion resistance; they also note that obtaining high-quality laser-clad coatings on magnesium alloys is difficult due to the substrate's low melting and boiling points.
item.future_work: The authors propose that future selection of high-entropy alloy compositions for laser cladding should be based on whether the same alloy prepared by arc melting exhibits excellent corrosion performance; if so, it is a candidate, otherwise it should not be selected.
quotes: The coating was composed of a simple FCC solid solution phase with a microhardness about 3.7 times higher than that of the AZ91D matrix.
The former was abrasive wear and the latter was adhesive wear.
The presence of Cr, Al, and Ni in the Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy coating prepared by laser cladding could form dense chromium oxides, aluminum oxides, and nickel oxides at the surface.
